newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK legislature starts work under legal cloud.
newsitem.headline: New HK legislature starts work under legal cloud.

text.p: Hong Kong's new legislature, its legitimacy already under challenge in court, is expected to take up emotive issues ranging from child immigration to rolling back worker-friendly laws at its opening session on Wednesday.
The 60-member legislature, appointed by Beijing, was sworn in last week after Britain surrendered this super-rich financial centre to Communist China, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Pro-democracy activists have denounced the new Provisional Legislature, which replaced an elected colonial assembly, and a string of court challenges are expected to test its legality.

"The body is unlawful, unconstitutional and invalid. Until the courts rule, we will have a cloud hanging over Hong Kong's judicial system," Raymond Wacks, law professor at the University of Hong Kong, told Reuters.
The new legislators have said they would press ahead with an array of laws, as well as considering the amendment or repeal of legislation rammed through in the dying days of British rule.
A bill permitting the deportation of hundreds of children to mainland China as illegal immigrants is one of the first laws which is expected to be considered by the legislature.
"The law about mainland children will certainly be an urgent issue," said Tsang Yok Sing, the leader of the pro- China DAB party.

Hong Kong has been inundated with young illegal immigrants from China over the past year. Newspaper reports that the new law might be retroactive to July 1 set pro-democracy supporters' teeth on edge.
"Not only is this an illegitimate body but it has set out immediately to behave in an illegal way," said Minky Worden, an assistant to pro-democracy leader Martin Lee.
Lee and other pro-democracy activists plan to stage a "Day of Mourning" protest outside the legislature building in central Hong Kong during Wednesday's session.
The protest will condemn the new Provisional Legislature and former lawmakers in the ousted colonial assembly are expected to attend, Worden said.
Lee's Democratic Party, which held 19 seats in the colonial legislature, refused to take part in the selection process for the new Beijing-appointed assembly.
The assembly is also expected to consider repealing parts of worker-friendly laws pushed through at the end of colonial rule, and to adopt a voting law for legislative elections next year.
The Provisional Legislature, which met in China before the end of colonial rule, was a constant source of friction between Britain and Beijing.
The last colonial governor, Chris Patten, held the most democratic legislative election in Hong Kong's history in 1995, in a move which provoked China's ire.

Beijing said Patten's electoral reforms violated previous Sino-British accords, vowed to dissolve the elected assembly after regaining Hong Kong and promptly did so just after midnight on June 30, cutting short the council's four-year term.
Legal challenges have already begun in an attempt to have the Provisional Legislature declared illegal, and an appeal court will hold a hearing on the first challenge on July 29.
In the case, lawyers have sought to halt a criminal case concerning corruption on grounds that a legal vacuum exists.

"All sides are very eager to have these challenges to the Provisional Legislature's validity heard as quickly as possible. Most people don't want to see our legal system in chaos," said political columnist Andy Ho.
